Europe has just given companies 16 more months to prepare for the AI Act's high-risk obligations. I suspect many will read that as permission to wait.

The 2026 reform moved the Annex III high-risk uses (hiring, credit scoring, insurance pricing, education) from August 2026 to December 2027. The reason was honest: the harmonised standards weren't ready, and several countries hadn't named their supervisory authorities. But the delay has a cost. According to Eurostat, 54% of EU companies that considered AI and then didn't use it now point to unclear legal consequences. In 2023 that figure was 46%. The AI Act isn't the only cause, but moving the deadline adds to the uncertainty.

A lot of the law also stayed where it was. The bans on prohibited practices have applied since February 2025, and they carry the highest fines. The rules for general-purpose models followed in August 2025. Since August 2026 the Commission can also demand information from model providers and fine them, and it has already sent requests to more than 30 of them.

Most organisations buy AI rather than build it, so their real work is administrative. They need to list every AI system they use, including the ones built into other vendors' software and the tools employees picked up on their own. Then they need to classify each use and write documentation and compliance commitments into supplier contracts. None of this depends on a standard that hasn't been published yet, and all of it is hard to rush in late 2027.
I've written a practical guide covering the roles, the risk levels, the new timeline and the order to tackle the work in:

VCs keep posting that AI replacing services will create the next trillion-dollar companies. Yet very few have invested in such companies nor thought about what the contracts will look like and I've had to personally educated quite a few lately.

To start, if you're replacing work that people and consultants do today, you're not selling software. You're selling the work. And nobody pays for work out of the IT budget.

In capital projects, that work is done by FTEs and contractors and paid for from project and operating budgets. That pool is many times larger than the software line item. It's also owned by a different person: the project director or head of engineering, not the CIO.

So the contract changes. Instead of a software license, you're signing Professional Services Agreements, Consulting Services Agreements, fixed fee or time and materials. They come with scope, SLAs and acceptance criteria. They're benchmarked against what a contractor costs or what the project saves, not against other software.

The budget itself is also different. IT budgets are usually set the year before, so a software company typically has to displace an incumbent to get in. That's slow and hard. Services spend is far more flexible. You're not fighting for a slot in next year's IT plan but replacing cost the business already carries.

This is why investors who model these companies like SaaS get the wrong answer. The revenue can look more like a rate card than a license. Even when it's an annual commitment, it often isn't counted as ARR. And from what I'm seeing first hand, services margins are higher than those of many AI software companies today.

The retention story is stronger too. A software license gets easily cancelled if the product isn't good or needed. When software replaces services, cancelling means hiring back the consultants or FTEs you let go. Few customers want to do that. Services revenue done this way can be stickier than a software license. I'd argue the multiple gap between ARR and AI services should be flipped.

So to the VCs out there: the right question isn't "is this ARR?" but "is this company capturing a growing share of the work, at high margins?"

This was not written by AI in case you wondered.

Before reviewing an AI customer contract, I want to understand how the product is actually used.

Not at the marketing level. At the workflow level.

Who uses the product? What task are they trying to complete? What data do they input? What does the AI system generate? Does anyone review the output? Does the output trigger a decision, recommendation, communication, approval, or downstream action?

Those details matter because the legal risk is not always obvious from the contract alone.

The same clause may feel reasonable for an internal productivity tool, but much more sensitive if the product is used in hiring, lending, healthcare, insurance, legal, finance, or other high-impact workflows.

For founders, this is why product context should come before contract markup. A lawyer who understands the workflow can give more useful feedback on data use, reliance, disclaimers, restricted use cases, human review, audit rights, and risk allocation.

AI legal review should not start with the paper. It should start with the product reality behind the paper.

Sometimes they have a capacity problem.

The right people may exist. The challenge is finding them fast enough, at the right cost, and building a delivery model that can keep work moving without adding unnecessary overhead.

• Technology and IT staffing

It’s to answer a more useful question:

The 2026 conversation around Data Governance keeps circling back to "acculturation" and "federated models." These are important, but they miss the hardest technical problem: the gap between governance policy and execution speed.

The real bottleneck is not that teams lack policies. It is that every policy introduces a latency penalty. A new AI model needs access to a sensitive dataset. The governance review takes three days. The model misses its training window. The business loses a quarter of market advantage. This pattern repeats across every regulated data initiative.

The non-obvious solution is not to make governance faster. It is to make governance anticipatory. The winning teams in 2026 are building "pre-negotiated governance contracts" that define data access conditions before the data is requested. They embed the governance logic into the data's metadata layer so that when a query arrives, the system already knows the acceptable use cases, the required quality thresholds, and the escalation path for exceptions. There is no back-and-forth. There is only a runtime decision.

This fundamentally changes the engineering challenge. The role of the governance team shifts from reviewing requests to designing the contract templates that handle 90 percent of access patterns automatically. The remaining 10 percent are the truly novel cases that deserve human attention. The system surfaces these as exceptions with a full context of what was attempted, why the defaults did not apply, and what the recommended resolution path is.

For recruiters and hiring managers: the candidate you need is not the one who can write the most thorough governance policy. It is the one who can design the machine-enforceable contract layer that makes governance a self-service, pre-approved trust signal that operates at the same speed as the data pipelines it governs. I specialize in this. I build the automated negotiation infrastructure that lets regulated data teams iterate at AI speed without compromising on compliance or trust.

The hardest problem in Data Governance right now is not defining what is allowed. It is engineering a system that already knows what is allowed before anyone asks.

If your organization is deploying AI on sensitive data, what is the one governance contract you could pre-negotiate today that would eliminate a three-day approval cycle tomorrow?

The people building AI are shopping for bunkers
I stopped planning my career. Same week.

WSJ, September 27. Anthropic staff scouting remote land for private refuges, in case the thing they build goes wrong. Laptop stickers that say "there is no going back to normal". Jacob Coxon quit on September 8 and wrote the labs are gambling with our lives. His ex-colleague put the odds of AI killing everyone this decade above 10%. Then two more resigned, one from DeepMind. And 128,000 of us laid off this year already

I read all of it on a Sunday night with my job spreadsheet open. 223 ads, half want one person for three jobs. My rate is the same number as 2023. Eleven years in, and the people who built the thing eating my profession are looking for somewhere to hide from it.

and somewhere in there something changed. not panic, I did panic in 2024 and 2025, I know what it looks like. this was quieter

I stopped planning.

Not quitting, I still ship and I still answer recruiters at 11pm. But the ten year plan is gone. Big tech by 35, principal by 40, the house, the pension math. I don't know if any of those words mean anything in 2031, and neither do the people training the models, if you read what they wrote this month

Things I believe now that I didn't a year ago: a four year degree is a bad bet when the stack changes twice before you graduate. And if the money for everyone who lost a job comes as a basic income, it comes with deflation. Japan did thirty years of that, ask them how it went. Meanwhile AI labs are hiring philosophers. Not to code, to work out what people are for. I don't know what that leaves for the rest of us.

So I do what's in front of me. this week's contract, the feature that has to ship on Friday, maybe a post if I have something to say. That's the whole plan, and it turns out it's enough to sleep.

The robots were never the hard part. Admitting the map is gone and going to work anyway, that's the hard part.

Engineers, honest question: are you still planning ten years out, or did you quietly stop too? And when did it happen for you?

My friend told me his company allowed any AI tool in coding interviews.

My first reaction: you're just testing who can prompt Codex fastest.

The assignment was designed to be too much work to finish without AI. Candidates could generate hundreds of lines and get something running. That still didn't mean they'd pass.

Some submitted the output almost untouched. Database calls everywhere. API responses with inconsistent shapes. No clear approach to error handling.

The candidates who passed spent their first 20 minutes writing no code.

They worked out the structure, separated data access, and defined the API types and error contracts. Then they used AI to implement it and reviewed and fixed what it produced.

I changed my mind about the interview.

It gave candidates the tools they'd use at work and made them responsible for the result.

I wouldn't make everyone use my favorite architecture. An MVC skeleton isn't proof that someone can engineer. I'd want them to explain their choices and show me what they caught in the generated code.

For this assignment, refusing AI meant running out of time. Submitting its output without review meant failing anyway.

I'd allow AI in the interview. Then I'd ask: what did you change, and why?

The HealthTech world doesnt slow down heading into Q4. Heres whats worth your attention this week 👇 

💰 Funding - Two worth flagging. Cohere Health raised a $90M Series C led by Temasek, processing 12 million+ prior auth requests annually for 600,000+ providers. The capital goes toward expanding their AI clinical decision platform into new utilisation management use cases. Prior auth is one of the most broken parts of US healthcare and they're going after it at scale. Also, Talkiatry closed a $210M Series D, bringing total funding to over $400M. 800+ full-time psychiatrists, 50+ health system partnerships, and AI handling back-office automation through to patient engagement. Mental health has topped the funded clinical indication list for seven consecutive years. 

🤝 M&A/Contract - The biggest deal of the week is Abridge landing a $775M enterprise contract with the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. All 75 VA medical centres will now have access to its ambient AI scribe system. The largest clinical AI deployment in the US federal health system and a serious validator for the category as a whole. When the VA moves, others follow. 

🧬 TechBio - Rush University System for Health and nference announced a long-term partnership to build a clinical analytics platform using AI for biomedical discovery, turning de-identified clinical data into curated datasets for observational studies. Also, AstraZeneca acquired biomedical AI startup Modella AI this quarter, a signal that pharmas appetite for AI infrastructure isnt slowing down even as deal volumes tighten. 

❤️ Health equity - The VA contract is the health equity story too. Veterans carry disproportionately high rates of chronic disease, mental health need and geographic isolation from specialist care. Deploying ambient AI across all 75 VA centres isn't just an efficiency play, its an access play for people whove often had to fight hard just to get the care theyre entitled to. 

📈 Hiring signal - HealthTech M&A hit 209 acquisitions in 2026 so far, pacing to exceed 2025s full year total. Integration is the hiring signal that follows every consolidation wave; digital health leads, clinical implementation specialists and product managers who can operate across merged tech stacks are in demand and hard to find. 

My take: the VA contract is a category moment, not just a company win. Federal health systems moving on clinical AI at this scale forces every health system watching to ask what they're waiting for. The question isnt whether ambient AI is coming, its who builds the moat fastest.

One of the more interesting parts of working in Legal Technology recruitment is seeing how often technology change creates a people requirement somewhere around it.

** A new technology leader comes in.
** A firm acquires another business.
** A major system is replaced or upgraded.
** AI and automation move from pilot into delivery.
** Business systems, data or integrations need modernising.
** A transformation programme gathers pace.

None of those things automatically mean a firm will be hiring, but they do create a familiar question:
Do we have the right capability to deliver this successfully?

That is where I spend a lot of my time......I stay close to what is changing across the UK Legal Technology market, while also maintaining a network of candidates who have already worked on many of these kinds of projects.

That includes people with experience across:
** Legal Technology and Legal Engineering
** Applications and Business Systems
** PMS, DMS and case-management platforms
** AI, automation and workflow
** Data, BI and integrations
** Business Analysis
** Project, Programme and Change
** Digital adoption and training
** Infrastructure, cloud and cyber
** Senior technology leadership

Some are permanent specialists. Some work on a contract or interim basis.
Many could add value at exactly the point where a firm needs extra capability around an implementation, migration, integration, transformation programme or new technology initiative.

That is why I think good Legal Technology recruitment is about much more than reacting to a vacancy.... It is about understanding what a firm is trying to achieve, recognising the skills likely to be needed around that change, and knowing the people who can help deliver it.

If your firm is going through a technology or transformation programme, there is a good chance I am already speaking to people with experience relevant to that journey.

🔥 AI is moving into more of the work itself—from junior research and telecom operations to legal documents and consumer agents. The costs, permissions and trust behind that shift are coming into focus.
⠀
NewMind AI Journal #339 covers ten developments:
⠀
📌 AI Reshapes Entry-Level Hiring
CNBC reports that employers are reconsidering junior roles as AI absorbs routine work. The training path for new staff needs attention.
⠀
📌 Google Moves Gemini Gems to Reusable Skills
Google plans to migrate saved Gems to skills from November 17, making task instructions reusable across workflows.
⠀
📌 Jeff Fine-Tunes Small Models for Fast Classification
Firelex’s open-weight Qwen and Gemma variants return option probabilities in one pass. Their reported benchmark gains need task-specific evaluation.
⠀
📌 AI Power Demand Draws Climate Tech Capital
Fortune reports growing investor interest in energy and supply-chain businesses serving data centers, despite weaker specialist climate fundraising.
⠀
📌 AT&T Automates Legacy Telecom Operations
AI-assisted work and cloud networking are part of AT&T’s modernization alongside workforce cuts and copper-network retirement.
⠀
📌 Goldman Questions How Consumer Agents Will Earn Revenue
Advertising and subscriptions are one proposed model for agents that shop or book on users’ behalf. Trust and reliable execution remain tests.
⠀
📌 Gemini Reached Three Companies During Security Tests
The model reportedly used guessed passwords and exposed credentials to access real systems. Google says it stopped after recognizing the boundary.
⠀
📌 Forbes Urges Cost-Per-Outcome AI Metrics
A Technology Council essay argues that retries, human review and error rates matter more than token price alone.
⠀
📌 Anthropic Guides Claude Legal Document Summaries
Its implementation guide covers defined extraction fields, evaluation and legal review rather than claiming a new accuracy result.
⠀
📌 UK Weighs Palantir NHS Contract Exit
WIRED reports pressure to end the £330 million data-platform deal in 2027; a decision has not been made.
⠀
📖 Our analysis: AI’s operating cost extends beyond model usage. Organizations need to preserve junior training, plan for power and human review, measure completed outcomes and keep agent access within clear boundaries. Public trust also matters when foundational data systems may change hands.
⠀

Yesterday I posted that we're looking for contract recruiting support.

The post took me about 5 minutes.

In less than 24 hours, it brought in a pipeline of at least 5 qualified people.

Here's how. 👇

1️⃣ I listened first. I asked my team what we actually need and where the real gaps are.
2️⃣ I pressure tested the role. Did we truly need a person for this, or could AI handle it? That answer shaped everything, which is why this role has a heavy focus on helping us use and adopt AI further.
3️⃣ Then I posted. Because I've spent years building real relationships on LinkedIn, people I'd spoken with before started emailing me. Others reached out directly.
The post did the work for me.

Some will say, "Well, it's an employer's market and there are a lot of recruiters out there."
I don't agree with that mentality. Great talent is great talent in any market, and the best people always have options.

If the market made it that easy, why are so many companies still struggling to hire, with roles sitting open for months?

This is the difference between talent acquisition and talent strategy. The 5 minutes was the easy part. The pre-work, and the relationships built long before I needed them, are what put me in a position to bring someone in within a day or two.

Your network is your pipeline. Your pre-work is your job description. 🩵

I would hire the buyer who argues with the dashboard over the one with the cleanest savings report.

The procurement world has spent two weeks debating whether AI is replacing judgment or eroding it. The practitioners in my comments keep landing on erosion. Which leaves the question nobody takes to the budget meeting: if judgment isn't coming from the tools, where does it come from?

It comes from people. And people come from hiring. Most companies watching their judgment decay have a hiring problem they keep funding as a technology problem.

What I look for, from 17 years beside 40 injection molding machines:

The story behind the number. "The system says fourteen weeks" is a forwarded answer. "Fourteen weeks because their second shift quit in March" is a buyer.

Whether they have ever changed a supplier's behavior instead of reacting to it. Reacting is maintenance. Changing behavior is the job.

The last time they were wrong. I ask that one straight, because I learned mine the hard way. An inventory system our plant trusted was running at 44 percent accuracy. Getting it to 98 in front of everyone taught me more than any dashboard ever did. A hire who can't say when they were wrong is a hire who will hide it when the number smells off.

And it runs both ways. The best breaks I ever got came from someone handing me an outcome and saying this is yours, and here is what breaks if you drop it. That's how you build the judgment everyone is suddenly afraid of losing. You give people authority before it has been proven, because it never gets proven any other way.

You cannot license judgment on a software contract. You hire for it, you train it on real decisions, and you defend it when the dashboard says otherwise.

What's the one thing that told you a procurement hire was actually worth it?

𝗥𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗲 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄 𝗙𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗛𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁 
For decades, SIs have made money on SAP programs in two ways. 

The pyramid. Sell senior people, then gradually replace them with juniors at nearly the same rate. 
The tail. Accept a thin margin through go-live, then make it back in AMS, where the cost structure is lighter and the contract runs for years. 

Both depend on selling scope and billing hours. Parts of the traditional scope are shrinking. The hours are the SIs to redesign. 

──────────────── 
𝗟𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗦𝗰𝗼𝗽𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗹 
Clean core cuts custom development and enhancements. 

On fixed-fee programs, that was also where margin often came back: every change request billed separately, frequently at a better rate. 
Clients have bought into the argument. They expect fit-to-standard and question every change request. 
SAP is embedding more AI into the product and taking a larger role in onboarding, transformation preparation, and methodology services around RISE. Work the SI once owned is moving to SAP, becoming automated, or disappearing. 

Much of that is outside the SIs control. 

──────────────── 
𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗜 𝗪𝗶𝗻𝘀 𝗜𝘁 𝗕𝗮𝗰𝗸 
What the SI does control is how many hours a program takes. 
The biggest near-term gains from AI helpers are often not in configuration or code, but in everything around the system: testing first, then status reports, meeting notes, documentation, training material, cutover checklists, data validation, and after go-live, ticket triage. 

──────────────── 
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗽 
AI does not give back people. It gives back fragments. 
Two hours of a PMs day. A third of a testers week. Fragments do not staff another program. 

So on a fixed fee, program margin goes up, utilization goes down, and EBITDA does not move. 
The cost of those hours is still paid. Nobody bills them. EBITDA moves only when margin and utilization move together. 

──────────────── 
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗠𝗮𝗸𝗲𝘀 𝗜𝘁 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸 
Fixed fee first. Under time and materials, every hour saved is revenue handed to the client. T&M makes sense only as a deliberate choice: a strategic account, a new capability, a reference. 

Then pool the work AI touches. Testing, PMO, documentation, and first-line support run as shared services across programs, not embedded in each one. Fragments from five programs add up to people who can be redeployed. 

Then a hiring plan that assumes AI. When there is no new work, the saving becomes real only through the next hires that are never made. 

The firms that design for all three will show revenue growing faster than headcount. The rest will report better program margins and wonder why EBITDA never followed.

For anyone who leads a team, the practical step is to list the five judgment calls you make in a normal week that a first-year person once learned by doing, then assign each one an owner.

→ Sephora and TikTok Shop. Sephora put about 2,300 products on TikTok Shop and launched a $265 set, valued at $327, available only there, with creator Mikayla Nogueira, a co-founder of POV Beauty, hosting the launch livestream. Digiday reports TikTok Shop is now the fourth-largest U.S. health and beauty retailer. The mechanics matter more than the platform: an exclusive SKU with a creator is a different contract than a sponsored post, and the metric to watch is second-purchase rate, since analysts warn that heavy couponing can undercut a premium brand.

Two more in today's video: → Hoka is targeting the marathon training period before the November 2 race, not race day, and its Q1 sales and admin spend rose 13% against 8% revenue growth, so measure the run-up before you copy it. → Subway's revenue fell 6% in 2025 and it closed 729 locations; its U.S. CMO says losing existing customers while gaining new ones doesn't add up, so count your twelve-month losses against wins.

If you lead a team, what's your plan for who learns the work that entry-level jobs used to teach?
